title: Griotte: Verified Compartmentalisation via Capabilities
abstract: CHERIoT is a novel hardware-software co-design that leverages hardware capabilities to define a notion of compartment, in a minimalistic capability-based OS, CHERIoT RTOS. By default, compartments are isolated to limit damage in case of bugs or malicious behaviour. To allow cross-compartment communication, the OS provides a privileged component, called the switcher. The switcher provides an interface for cross-compartment calls, while enforcing isolation between compartments and guaranteeing stack safety. Together with hardware capabilities, the switcher is critical to enforce the security guarantees of the CHERIoT compartment model. The design of CHERIoT raises two questions: First, how can one formalise the informal notion of compartmentalisation that CHERIoT compartments are designed to provide? And second, given that the safety properties of CHERIoT hinge on the complementary roles of the capability machine and of the switcher, does the design of CHERIoT enforce the desired security properties? In this paper, we introduce Griotte and Griotte OS, idealised but faithful versions of the CHERIoT machine and the CHERIoT RTOS, which we use to answer these two questions: First, we formally capture the aforementioned security guarantees in the form of a continuation-based logical relation which captures the combined behaviour of the switcher and of the capability machine. And second, we define a specification for the Griotte switcher that enforces those guarantees, and prove that the implementation meets the specification. We demonstrate Griotte on a range of key scenarios illustrating different aspects of CHERIoT, including integrity of the local state in the presence of memory sharing with unknown code. Our approach is modular: we verify compartments individually, and then compose their specifications. Together, our contributions give a solid formal foundation to the design of CHERIoT.

title: User Representation via Cross Multi-source Behavior Pre-training for Mobile Games
abstract: User representation pre-training has become a fundamental paradigm for alleviating data sparsity in downstream personalization tasks. However, existing studies predominantly focus on single-app or app-level behaviors, overlooking the inherently cross-source and multi-granular nature of user activities on mobile devices. At the device level, user intent emerges from complex interactions among heterogeneous behavior sources and hierarchical action structures, posing challenges that cannot be addressed by conventional app-centric modeling. To tackle this issue, we propose CM-PTM, a novel Cross Multi-source Behavior Pre-Training Model tailored for mobile game user representation learning on device-level behavioral logs. CM-PTM employs hierarchical cascaded mask-then-predict proxy tasks that first infer the source of the next behavior and then progressively refine predictions at the app-action level. This design enables unified modeling of cross-source dependencies and fine-grained behavioral dynamics within a single pre-training paradigm. Extensive experiments on large-scale real-world mobile datasets demonstrate that CM-PTM effectively captures users' endogenous interests and consistently delivers significant performance gains on downstream mobile game recommendation tasks.

title: Can Scene Text Recognition Read Rare Compositions?
abstract: Scene text recognition is reported as 89--97% accurate on the six standard benchmarks, and the problem is widely treated as saturated. We present an alternative reading. When the same test images are stratified jointly by ground-truth word rarity and character n-gram novelty against a reference corpus, accuracy at the rare-word x rare-trigram corner of the resulting 5x5 grid drops 10--18 pt below the q3/q3 centre across nine English specialised recognisers, and the same direction (corner below centre) holds on all 13 of 13 (language, model) pairs we test across four writing systems (Latin, Han, Han+kana, Arabic). The drop is not a capacity bottleneck. A 6x vision-backbone scale-up (CLIP4STR-Base 158M -> CLIP4STR-Huge 1.0B, OpenCLIP ViT-H/14 LAION-2B) leads every benchmark in aggregate accuracy yet leaves the stress corner unchanged (86.9 -> 86.5, within paired-bootstrap noise). Four converging probes--layer-wise probing, confidence-when-wrong, attention re-balancing, and a cross-script commit-vs-abstain error split--localise the failure to the autoregressive decoder's lexical prior. We then ask how much of the gap existing techniques recover. Of 16 non-architectural mitigations, the largest mean q5/q5 gain is +1.3 pt and none clears the paired-bootstrap noise floor; the only intervention that does is the architectural shift from autoregressive to CTC decoding (SVTRv2, +2.5 pt, p=0.02, n=474). A confidence-routed AR-CTC ensemble adds a directionally consistent +0.6 pt that stays within noise, and its dominant learned coefficient is each model's own minimum-softmax confidence--independently echoing the mechanism above. No configuration we test improves both the compositional corner and aggregate accuracy. The rare-input long tail thus points to architectural change rather than added capacity.

title: UAV-borne Magnetic and Radiometric Data: Advancing Processing, Fusion, Machine Learning, and Inversion
abstract: Uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) magnetic and gamma-ray spectrometric surveys can collect geophysical data at higher spatial density than conventional airborne systems. This makes them useful for geological mapping and mineral exploration at local scales. However, added detail does not automatically lead to better geological interpretation. UAV measurements are affected by detector footprint, terrain, flight geometry, sampling, counting uncertainty, and spatial dependence. This thesis examines how these factors control the geological information recovered from UAV magnetic and radiometric surveys. The first part investigates UAV-borne gamma-ray spectrometry. It evaluates how terrain, detector height, and platform motion influence radiometric measurements. It also develops a terrain-correction approach that accounts for source-detector geometry and terrain visibility. The results show that acquisition effects can produce spatial patterns that resemble geological variation if they are not considered during processing and interpretation. The thesis then introduces RadSIMU, a survey-scale simulation framework for UAV-borne gamma-ray spectrometry. The simulator tests how flight speed, line spacing, integration time, terrain, and detector footprint affect spatial feature recovery. The results show that recoverable detail is mainly controlled by detector footprint and sampling density. Longer integration times reduce counting noise, but they do not recover information lost through footprint averaging or undersampling. Building on this physical understanding, a terrain-aware inversion method is developed to estimate near-surface radioelement distributions from UAV gamma-ray data. The inversion links airborne measurements to surface radioelement concentrations through a forward model that includes detector footprint, attenuation, terrain visibility, acquisition geometry, and measurement uncertainty. The recovered models improve spatial interpretation and show the resolution limits imposed by measurement physics. also evaluates supervised machine learning for lithological mapping using UAV magnetic and radiometric predictors. It shows that random validation can overestimate performance when spatial dependence is present. Spatial validation gives a more realistic assessment of predictive skill. Finally, radiometric evidence is used to evaluate geological constraints applied in magnetic inversion. The results show that such constraints should be treated as testable geological interpretations rather than fixed representations of the subsurface. Overall, this thesis provides a connected framework for understanding, recovering, and evaluating geological information from UAV-borne magnetic and radiometric data.

title: AI explained: a guide for non-technical readers
abstract: AI Explained: A Guide for Non-Technical Readers builds understanding of artificial intelligence from first principles rather than diving in at the top. Written by experienced policy and technical experts, the book walks through rules and logic-based approaches, statistical methods, neural networks, machine learning, and generative models in accessible, structured terms. Each major section concludes with a dedicated use-cases chapter grounding abstract concepts in practical scenarios drawn from healthcare, law, and business. Rather than teaching readers how to build or deploy AI, the book answers a more fundamental question: how do these systems achieve the outcomes they produce? Coverage of AI policy, ethics, and societal impact rounds out the treatment, informed directly by the authors' advisory roles with governments and international bodies.

title: Dodging impossibilities in quantum cryptography : on the feasibility of one-time programs, signing quantum states, and cryptography without one-way functions
abstract: Cette thèse par articles étudie les frontières de la faisabilité cryptographique quantique, en démontrant comment les propriétés singulières de l’information quantique peuvent être exploitées pour contourner des résultats d’impossibilité fondamentaux. Nous explorons trois régimes distincts dans lesquels des théorèmes d’impossibilité (≪ No-Go ≫) traditionnels sont surmontés : la réalisation de programmes à usage unique dans un modèle où la mémoire quantique de l’adversaire est de taille bornée, la signature de messages quantiques au moyen de contraintes temporelles et la réalisation de primitives cryptographiques sans avoir à supposer l’existence de fonctions à sens unique. La première partie de ce travail exploite le modèle de mémoire quantique bornée (Bounded Quantum Storage Model ), dans lequel les adversaires sont limités quant à leur mémoire quantique. Nous démontrons que cette limitation physique permet la construction de programmes à usage unique — une forme puissante d’obfuscation de programmes dont l’impossibilité est prouvée dans le modèle standard. De manière cruciale, puisque la sécurité découle de contraintes de mémoire plutôt que de difficulté calculatoire, nos constructions atteignent une sécurité au sens de la théorie de l’information. Nous utilisons les programmes à usage unique pour développer, pour la première fois, des applications cryptographiques fondamentales, notamment le chiffrement à clé asymétrique et les signatures numériques assortis de garanties au sens de la théorie de l’information. La deuxième contribution remet en question le paradigme établi de longue date selon lequel la signature de messages quantiques est intrinsèquement impossible. Nous introduisons les signatures dépendantes du temps, dont la sécurité est assurée par la synchronisation temporelle des processus de signature et de vérification. Nous montrons que ce cadre permet la signature d’états quantiques à l’aide de n’importe quelle fonction à sens unique et puzzle à verrou temporel (time-lock puzzle). De plus, nous démontrons qu’en recourant à des clés de vérification dynamiques qui évoluent au cours du temps, l’exigence de puzzles à verrou temporel peut être éliminée. Nous appliquons le schéma de signature à la construction du chiffrement à clé publique quantique authentifié dépendant du temps et de la monnaie quantique à clé publique. La dernière partie de la thèse contribue au corpus croissant de recherches réévaluant la nécessité fondamentale des fonctions à sens unique (OWF) en tant qu’hypothèse inimale pour une cryptographie non triviale. Plus précisément, nous fournissons une séparation en boîte noire démontrant qu’un générateur pseudo-aléatoire (PRG) augmenté d’une procédure d’échantillonnage d’entrée quantique représente une hypothèse potentiellement plus faible qu’un PRG traditionnel à échantillonnage uniforme, lequel est équivalent aux OWF. À partir de cette observation, nous montrons que des applications importantes, telles que l’authentification de messages et les mises en gage (commitments) avec communication classique, sont également séparées en boîte noire des PRG traditionnels. Cela apporte des éléments en faveur d’une nouvelle hypothèse, potentiellement plus faible, pour ces applications cryptographiques. Prises ensemble, ces contributions offrent une perspective différente des paysages dans lequel le cryptographie quantique peut-être développée. En remplaçant les hypothèses fondamentales — de la difficulté calculatoire vers des bornes de mémoire, de l’indépendance temporelle vers la dépendance temporelle, et de l’échantillonnage uniforme vers l’échantillonnage quantique — cette thèse établit qu’une gamme plus large de primitives sûres est faisable dans des modèles réalistes que ce qui est possible dans le modèle calculatoire standard.

title: The Cardinality Ceiling: Why Agentic LLM Output Succeeds on Low-Constraint Requests and Degrades as Constraint Cardinality Rises
abstract: This paper describes a process as it is. It makes one descriptive claim: agentic large language model (LLM) output is well-suited to requests that carry few simultaneously-binding constraints, and it degrades in a predictable, enumerable way as the number of such constraints rises. The paper does not argue that practitioners should change their behavior or that products should change their design. It provides a mechanical account of why the degradation occurs, an account of why the degradation is difficult to observe in current practice, and an ordered list of the specific failure modes that appear as constraint cardinality increases. The account is grounded in first-person practitioner experience, including a documented multi-week loss and its later one-day resolution under changed constraints, and in a live design session that produced several of the enumerated failures in real time.

title: Code and processed datasets for "Lightweight fine-tuning of ECG-FM transfers to eight ICU/ED prediction tasks"
abstract: This repository accompanies the PLOS ONE manuscript "Lightweight fine-tuning of ECG-FM transfers to eight ICU/ED prediction tasks". It provides the code and processed (de-identified, subject-level) datasets required to reproduce the benchmark of a lightweight fine-tuning of the open ECG-FM foundation model across eight critical-care prediction tasks (pulmonary embolism, atrial fibrillation, shock, troponin elevation, long-QT, cardiac arrest, in-hospital mortality, and hyperkalemia) on MIMIC-IV-ECG and eICU-CRD.

title: Adaptive Probabilistic Logic Programming
abstract: This paper introduces Adaptive Probabilistic Logic Programming (APLP), a novel approach to intelligent systems design. The core challenge in many real-world applications is dealing with uncertainty and evolving environments. Traditional logic programming suffers from rigidity, requiring explicit definition of all rules upfront, which is often impractical and brittle. APLP addresses this limitation by dynamically adapting probabilistic logic rules based on observed execution outcomes. This is achieved through the integration of Bayesian Networks for representing uncertainty and probabilistic logic inference engines. The system iteratively updates its rules using a Monte Carlo method for decision making. The key innovation lies in the ability of the system to learn and optimize its rules in response to changing data, leading to enhanced robustness and adaptability. This paper outlines the architecture, the key components, and the core mechanism of APLP, demonstrating its potential for applications requiring intelligent decision-making in dynamic and uncertain scenarios. The system's adaptability is central to its performance, allowing it to respond effectively to unforeseen circumstances.

title: 形式逻辑底层第一性关系公理体系
abstract: 本文依托元基-三维元系统-双层复合系统核心公理,构建逻辑学底层统一形式体系。定义全域唯一第一性关系:顶层元系统(定义域D)主导、底层元系统(调制域M),底层无法改写顶层本体属性;依托投射、析出、序化、模态化、闭包五类基础操作,可完整派生传统逻辑学全部七大类、二十种基础逻辑关系。结合五阶循环群建立逻辑模态环流结构,完成范畴论等价证明;对演绎、归纳、反证等全部经典推理规则实现底层溯源,以此提出全新人工智能分层逻辑范式。给出五条可检验形式逻辑猜想,其中极小元定理作为核心数学命题,为数理逻辑、模态逻辑、AI推理提供统一底层公理,实现社会组织、生物编码、微观粒子、基础逻辑全域拓扑统一

title: Canefield Rat: A Novel Metaheuristic Algorithm Inspired by Foraging Behavior
abstract: This paper introduces a novel metaheuristic algorithm, termed "Canefield Rat," inspired by the foraging behavior of *Canefield rats* (genus *Neotoma*). These rats are known for their efficient and adaptive strategies in locating and exploiting food sources in complex environments. The algorithm leverages key aspects of their foraging process, including path exploration, memory of successful locations, and probabilistic decision-making, to construct a robust optimization approach. Canefield Rat utilizes a population-based search strategy combined with a memory mechanism to guide the exploration and exploitation phases. The algorithm's core components involve a fitness function, a neighborhood structure, and a probabilistic acceptance criterion. We demonstrate the efficacy of Canefield Rat through a series of test problems, comparing its performance against established metaheuristic algorithms such as Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and Ant Colony Optimization (ACO). The results indicate that Canefield Rat exhibits competitive performance and offers a promising alternative for tackling various optimization challenges.

title: Title: Adaptive Resonance Network for Pattern Recognition (ARNP)
abstract: This paper presents the Adaptive Resonance Network (ARNP), a novel neural network architecture specifically designed for pattern recognition. The core innovation of ARNP lies in its dynamic weighting system, which allows the network to adapt its pattern recognition parameters based on the characteristics of the input data. This adaptive approach enhances robustness and accuracy compared to static pattern recognition methods. The paper details the architecture, training methodology, and experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of ARNP in various pattern recognition tasks. We explore the impact of the dynamic weighting system on the network's performance, highlighting its ability to generalize to unseen data.

title: Non-Linear Topological Geometry: Modeling Quantum Entanglement
abstract: This paper explores the potential of non-linear topological geometry to model quantum entanglement, focusing on its application to quantum information storage and processing. We propose a novel framework incorporating the concept of "quantum topological entanglement" – a dynamic and non-linear topological structure that interacts with quantum entanglement, offering a pathway toward enhanced quantum algorithms. The core mechanism involves constructing a model that dynamically evolves, leveraging the inherent properties of topological geometry to store and manipulate quantum information. We demonstrate the potential of this model through theoretical analysis and illustrative examples, suggesting significant advantages in quantum computation, particularly regarding information fidelity and entanglement generation.

title: 基于自适应的复杂系统模型生成的优化算法
abstract: This paper introduces a novel optimization algorithm based on adaptive systems models, designed to address the limitations of traditional optimization techniques in complex systems. The algorithm dynamically adjusts optimization strategies based on the system's complexity and initial state, providing a more flexible and powerful approach to model optimization. We propose a framework that leverages a hierarchical system model to represent the system, enabling the algorithm to progressively refine its optimization strategy. The paper details the design of the adaptive component, its implementation, and the results achieved through extensive simulations. We demonstrate that the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods in a variety of complex system optimization scenarios, showcasing its ability to effectively navigate intricate parameter spaces and achieve optimal solutions.
